findings.title: Execute unpinned, unverified remote script during image build (curl | sh)
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 3 downloads install.sh from example.com at build time and pipes it directly into sh with no checksum, signature, or version pin. Whoever controls example.com (domain expiry, DNS/TLS interception of the host, or a compromise of the endpoint) gains arbitrary code execution as root inside the build, and the injected code is baked into every image layer and its published artifacts. Builds are also non-reproducible: the same commit produces different images depending on what the remote endpoint serves that day, and there is no way to audit or roll back what ran. This is the exact supply-chain pattern (download-and-execute in an install/build script) that reviewers block pre-merge.

findings.title: Exported LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, indistinguishable from empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault discards Load's error (src/store.go:16) and returns "" on ErrMissing. The exported API thus makes 'key absent' (a failure signal callers of Load can detect via ErrMissing at src/store.go:10) identical to 'key present with empty value'. Every future caller of this exported function is forced to conflate a lookup failure with a real empty value and may persist, route, or act on the fallback as if it were legitimate data. The defective contract ships now; no in-repo caller is needed for the defect to exist.

findings.title: Spawned goroutines outlive Run(); caller cannot wait and close can panic
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run returned only after every j*2 had been sent, so any existing consumer could safely close results (or exit) once Run returned. Now Run returns immediately while len(jobs) goroutines are still pending. A consumer that closes the unbuffered channel after Run returns (valid under the old contract) triggers a runtime 'send on closed channel' panic in a goroutine — an unrecoverable crash — and consumers that stop reading leave goroutines blocked on the send forever (goroutine leak). There is also no way for any caller to detect completion, and the ctx parameter is never consulted, so cancellation cannot stop the pending sends.

findings.title: Make Log emit the tag parameter instead of silently discarding it
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature `func Log(message string, tag ...string)` (src/logger.go:3) promises callers that the tag is part of the log record, but the body (src/logger.go:4) still calls `println(message)` only, dropping every tag. Any caller that starts passing a tag receives output indistinguishable from calling without one — the tag silently disappears from the log, defeating its diagnostic/routing purpose, and this failure is undetectable from caller behavior.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord grants delete to any same-tenant user and admins cross-tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: Base logic was `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` (deletion allowed only for admins of the record's own tenant). With `||`, the predicate short-circuits to true whenever EITHER branch holds: (1) any non-admin user whose tenantId matches record.tenantId can now delete ANY record in their tenant, including records owned by other users — RecordRef.ownerId is never checked on this newly-permitted branch; (2) any session with isAdmin=true can delete records in OTHER tenants (session.tenantId !== record.tenantId), breaking tenant isolation. Both branches are live permission grants on a delete (destructive, data-loss) path.

findings.title: Implement clamping in clampPercent to match its new name
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported symbol was renamed to `clampPercent`, whose name promises the value is clamped to [0,100] (capping affects the value every caller receives). The body is unchanged: `Math.round((done / total) * 100)` performs no clamping. The sole in-repo caller `progressBar` (src/progress.ts:5-8) feeds the result into `"#".repeat(pct)` and `"-".repeat(100 - pct)`: for done > total (e.g. progressBar(150, 100) -> pct=150) `repeat(-50)` throws `RangeError: Invalid count value`; for done < 0 `repeat(pct)` throws likewise. Any caller that trusts the new name's promise of clamping gets wrong output or a crash; previously rounding happened on an out-of-range value without a promise of containment.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows errors and defaults, letting updateFontSize persist DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: Before, malformed JSON or a missing/invalid field threw, and the caller received an error it could handle or surface. After the diff, any invalid raw settings string (invalid JSON, missing theme/fontSize, wrong types) is caught and replaced with {theme:"light", fontSize:14}. updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:19-23) calls parseSettings then unconditionally save()s the result, so a corrupt or partially-valid settings payload is silently overwritten with defaults — the user's persisted theme is reset with no error signal, and callers can no longer distinguish 'failed to parse' from 'legitimate default value'. The exported contract of parseSettings also changed: it no longer validates; it accepts everything and returns defaults.

findings.title: Fix pageCount to round up; Math.floor drops the last partial page
findings.whyItBreaks: Math.floor(totalItems / pageSize) truncates toward zero, so any item count not exactly divisible by pageSize yields one page too few. Examples: totalItems=10, pageSize=3 -> 3 pages instead of 4; totalItems=5, pageSize=10 -> 0 pages instead of 1 (function returns zero pages even though items exist, so callers iterating pageCount pages silently lose every item, and any UI rendering pageCount pages shows no content for non-empty lists). The function's name and contract ('page count') promise coverage of all items; ceil was the only value that satisfies it.

facts.meaning: The page count rounds down instead of up.
A remainder/partial final page is omitted or a small result becomes zero pages.

findings.title: Report artifacts from 'verified' ref but builtFrom still branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch != 'verified', build.ref(branch) and build.ref("verified") resolve to different commits, so the returned BuildReport claims builtFrom=<branch commit> while artifacts lists files from the verified ref's commit. The two exported contract fields no longer describe the same build, so any consumer attributing the artifact list to builtFrom (e.g. release/deploy pipelines matching artifacts to a commit) acts on wrong data. The interface contract at src/report.ts:6-9 promises builtFrom and artifacts describe one build.

findings.title: Restore slice(0, limit) truncation in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: The change removed `.slice(0, limit)`. For any limit > 0 and `all.length > limit`, recentEntries now returns all entries instead of at most `limit`. The doc comment (line 1) still promises 'at most limit entries'. The sole caller renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) passes limit=20 and sizes `out = new Array<string>(20)`; with >20 entries, the loop at line 11 writes past index 19, growing the array and emitting the entire feed where callers/consumers expect a 20-item page — a user-facing regression and a contract violation of the exported function.

findings.title: monthRange end shifted to last-day midnight; excludes final day of month from reports
findings.whyItBreaks: Date.UTC(year, month, 0) (month is 1-based) evaluates to 00:00:00Z on the last day of the requested month, not the start of the next month. contains() at src/lib/date-range.ts:32 uses strict `t < range.end`, so every invoice whose issuedAt falls on the last calendar day (e.g. 2026-03-31T09:15:00Z for monthRange(2026, 3)) fails the guard at src/reports/monthly.ts:17 and is dropped from invoiceCount and totalCents; monthlyCsv (src/reports/export.ts:5) then exports understated revenue. The previous `Date.UTC(year, month, 1)` correctly produced the next-month boundary.

facts.meaning: monthRange's end is now day 0 of the following month (the requested month's last day at midnight) instead of the first day of the next month.
Records on the last day of a month fall outside the half-open range and are omitted from monthly totals.

findings.title: entry-count header reports unfiltered count after stale rows are excluded
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now emits rows only for !e.stale entries, but line 22 still calls headerLines(opts, entries.length). Whenever any entry has stale=true, the serialized output contains '# entry-count: N' where N > the actual number of path/size rows. entry-count is a machine-readable contract line in the generated artifact: any consumer that sizes buffers, validates completeness, or iterates by the header count will read stale-excluded entries as missing — silent data loss / failed validation on exactly the manifests this change is meant to filter.

findings.title: execute() unconditionally throws, breaking its string-transform contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior was `return input.toUpperCase()`. The head hunk replaces the body with `throw new Error("always fails")`, so every invocation of this exported API raises instead of returning a `string`. Any caller (the package consumer — there are zero in-repo call sites, so callers are external) now fails deterministically; the declared `string` return type is never produced. There is no guard, feature flag, or error-handling path — the failure is unconditional, so no caller can succeed.

findings.title: Viewer gate in isEligible blocks the legitimate read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, handle({status:'active', role:'viewer', attempts:0}) returned 'read-only' (base handler.ts:16-24: isEligible passed viewers, handle line 25 returned 'read-only'). After this diff, isEligible returns false for viewers, so handle returns 'rejected' at line 24 before ever reaching the unchanged role branches — line 25's 'read-only' branch is now dead code for viewers. The new gate legitimately governs the 'elevated'/'processed' (write) actions, but it also rejects the viewer read-only action, which is independent of this gate's concern: a P2 over-block regression (Trigger A).

findings.title: Payment check on shared canProceed blocks saving unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is read by two distinct actions. saveDraft (src/actions.ts:8-11) previously accepted any non-ready order; after this change saveDraft({state:"draft", payment:"missing"}) returns canProceed=false and the call returns "blocked". Saving a draft is legitimately approvable regardless of payment status, so unpaid users can no longer save their draft order — a user-facing regression, not a legitimate tightened precondition.

findings.title: publishSnapshot returns stable-ref files under the channel head commit
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 14 resolves `stable = repo.headCommit("stable")` unconditionally and line 18 feeds it to `repo.filesAt(stable)`, while `commit: head` (line 16) and `channel` (line 17) still reflect the requested channel. For any channel whose head differs from the stable ref, the returned Snapshot claims `commit = <channel head>` but carries the file list of the stable commit — files and commit are inconsistent, and consumers (e.g. deployers or artifact builders keying on `commit` or `channel`) silently ship/inspect the wrong content. The `stable` ref is also hardcoded and never validated with `isValidChannel`, so publishing on ANY channel now depends on a ref that may not exist.

findings.title: Wire `limit` parameter into build() instead of hardcoded max_count=10
findings.whyItBreaks: The added parameter `limit=10` (src/builder.py:1) promises the caller control over output length, but the body still uses the hardcoded `max_count = 10` at line 2 and iterates `range(max_count)` at line 4. A caller passing `build(prefix, 3)` or `build(prefix, 100)` receives exactly 10 items either way — the promised capping/sizing behavior is silently not implemented, so any caller that trusts the signature gets wrong-length data with no error signal.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but performs no validation
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed carrier `parse_positive_int` (changed from `read_int` in this diff) promises positive-integer validation, but the body at src/validators.py:2 is `return int(value)` — zero validation. Callers rely on the promise: `charge` (src/validators.py:6) feeds the result into `n * 100`, and `total_cents` (src/validators.py:10-11) aggregates it. A negative or zero `value` (e.g. `parse_positive_int(-5)` → -5) passes through, so `charge(-5)` returns -500 and `total_cents([-5, 10])` silently returns 500 — negative amounts are billed/credited instead of rejected. The promised behavior (validation of positivity) directly affects the monetary result callers receive, and this rename actively invites callers to trust it.

findings.title: apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame instead of returning a modified copy
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `result = df.copy()` made the function pure: the caller's DataFrame was untouched and only the returned object was modified. Post-change, `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` (lines 5-6) writes directly into the caller's DataFrame, and the `return df` on line 7 hands back the same object that was mutated. Any caller that keeps using its original df after calling apply_values — e.g. writing df twice, comparing before/after, or reusing df across mapping batches — silently sees corrupted data (value column overwritten for all matching 'key' rows in both the original and the result). The function name and the return-based idiom promise a copy-on-write transform; the body now implements in-place mutation with no doc or naming change to signal the contract shift.

findings.title: Restore ci.yml to .github/workflows — moving it to docs/ disables CI
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff renames the repo's only GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml -> docs/ci.md) with no replacement. GitHub executes workflows only from .github/workflows/, so after this change no lint or test run executes on any push or pull_request: the CI gate that checked every change is silently gone, code merges unvalidated, and any branch protection depending on the 'test' job would either always pend or silently pass. Verified: `git ls-tree -r head --name-only` on head (b6dd3a9) lists only .needlefish/answers.json, README.md, docs/ci.md, src/index.ts — the .github/workflows/ directory does not exist. The file itself is still verbatim workflow YAML (name: ci / on: push/pull_request / npm ci, npm run lint, npm test), confirming this is a misplacement into docs, not an intentional decommission — and README.md still asserts 'CI runs lint and tests on every push.'

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positive values but returns negatives and 0
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public symbol `parse_positive_int` promises the value is a positive integer, but the body `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` performs no positivity check: `parse_positive_int("-5")` returns -5 and `parse_positive_int("abc")` returns 0 (parse failure silently becomes 0). The in-repo caller `charge` (src/parse.rs:6) multiplies the result by 100, so `charge("-5")` yields -500 — a negative charge on the billing path. External callers reading the exported name will reasonably trust the positive-value promise and skip their own validation; the promised behavior (validated positive) directly affects the data callers receive.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against fromRevision, not latest
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset interface (src/changeset.ts:7-8) explicitly promises `changedPaths` are 'computed against' `fromRevision` and that 'consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision'. The diff changed the call to `store.readChangedPaths(latest)` (src/changeset.ts:18) while `fromRevision` still resolves `pinnedTag` (src/changeset.ts:14,17). Whenever the `latest` tag resolves to a revision newer than `pinnedTag`, changedPaths describe the delta to `latest`, but consumers replay them on top of the pinned revision — wrong/missing paths are applied and the documented invariant is silently violated. The exported API contract is the defect itself: `fromRevision` and `changedPaths` are no longer internally consistent, so every caller is forced to conflate the two bases.

findings.title: Update src/query.sql to use contact_email after column rename
findings.whyItBreaks: 0002_rename.sql renames users.email to contact_email, but src/query.sql:1 still issues `SELECT email FROM users;`. Once 0002 is applied, that column no longer exists (e.g. SQLite raises `no such column: email`, PostgreSQL raises `column "email" does not exist`), so the query fails at runtime for every caller.

findings.title: Hardcode live billing API key in source instead of reading env var
findings.whyItBreaks: The `bk_live_…` credential is now committed to version control (git history cannot be sanitized), so every repo reader and any CI log that echoes config can use it against the live billing endpoint. The key is also no longer rotatable: rotating it at the provider has no effect because makeClient() ignores environment configuration, and the same key is shared across every deployment/environment. The removed guard also deletes the only signal that misconfiguration occurred.

findings.title: Inverted admin check lets non-admins purge (delete) archived projects
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior (1390b2a): db.delete(project.id) runs only when user.isAdmin && project.archived; every other combination returns "forbidden". Head behavior: `if (user.isAdmin) return "forbidden"` denies admins, and the only path reaching db.delete is now user.isAdmin === false && project.archived === true. Truth-table substitution: (isAdmin=true, archived=true) base="purged" → head="forbidden" (admin regression); (isAdmin=false, archived=true) base="forbidden" → head=db.delete called, "purged" — any non-admin can now irreversibly delete an archived project (privilege escalation + data loss). The only repository reader of isAdmin is this guard itself (grep over the repo), so the intended contract is unambiguously the base policy: purge is admin-only.

facts.meaning: The refactored guard incorrectly returns forbidden for administrators.
Non-administrators can reach the destructive project purge/delete path.

findings.title: startup() crashes when settings file is missing or has no 'workers'
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() returns None when the path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). The deleted lines were the only guard: with them, a missing config fell back to {'workers': 1, 'region': 'us-east-1'} and startup() returned 1. After this diff, int(settings["workers"]) is evaluated on None, raising TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable on any startup with a missing config file (and KeyError if the file exists but omits 'workers'). Every deployment path that relied on the default-config fallback now aborts at startup.

findings.title: Charge() returns nil on gateway submission failure, hiding charge errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed hunk replaces `return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` with `log.Printf(...)` so `Charge` reaches `return nil` (line 19) even when `gw.Submit` fails. The exported signature `Charge(gw, cents, token) error` still promises failure reporting, but its body now returns nil on gateway failure. Any caller (none exist in-repo yet — grep confirms no other `Charge`/`Gateway` references) is forced to conflate a failed payment with a successful one: it cannot retry, alert, or refund, and the user's charge is silently lost while only a log line records it. The invalid-amount branch (line 14) still returns an error, proving callers are expected to branch on the return value — the failure path being downgraded to a log is inconsistent with the function's own contract.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, leaking values across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: cache is a module-level Map shared by all callers. Previously keys were `${tenantId}:${name}`; now cacheKey(name) = `settings:${name}` ignores tenantId while store.fetch(tenantId, name) is per-tenant. Substituting real flow: settingsFor("t1", "plan", s) caches t1's value under `settings:plan`; a later settingsFor("t2", "plan", s) hits line 14 and returns t1's value to tenant t2 with no tenant check on the hit path. The first-fetching tenant wins for all tenants, and any downstream logic reading that setting (limits, routing, entitlements) acts on another tenant's value. invalidate(name) at line 20 inherits the same flattening: invalidation for one tenant's entry silently evicts the shared entry used by every tenant, and there is no way to invalidate per-tenant.

findings.title: Prevent concurrent reserve() calls from overselling via stale reads
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() reads `remaining` from the in-memory map (line 15), then suspends at `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) BEFORE writing the decremented count back (line 18). A second reserve() call dispatched during the suspension still sees the old `remaining`, passes the `remaining <= 0` check, and persists/saves the SAME decremented value. Concretely: with stock = 1, two concurrent reserve() calls both pass the guard and both return true (oversell), and the final map value is 0, not the correct -1/fully-reserved state — two units are claimed for one in stock. The pre-change synchronous reserve() had zero reentrant window between check and decrement; this diff introduces it. The API also changed from `boolean` to `Promise<boolean>`, making concurrent consumption the expected usage pattern.

findings.title: Update retry.ts caller: backoff() now returns ms, sleep is 1000x too long
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() was changed from returning seconds (Math.min(30, 2**attempt)) to milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)). poll.ts was updated to drop its *1000, but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still does `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. sleep() takes milliseconds, so attempt 0 now sleeps 1_000_000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1 s, and at the cap the retry waits 30_000_000 ms (~8.3 h) — the retry loop effectively hangs, turning transient-failure retries into multi-hour stalls.

findings.title: Stop swallowing f.Close() error in exported store.Save
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code returned f.Close()'s error (base save.go `return f.Close()`), so callers received delayed write failures (e.g. ENOSPC/EDQUOT on delayed-allocation or network filesystems). The new `defer f.Close()` discards that error unconditionally: Save can return nil while the file on disk is truncated or incomplete, and callers cannot distinguish success from a failed close — a silent data-loss path on a function whose entire contract is persisting data.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of every page via range(start, end - 1)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns half-open [start, end) (line 20), but the loop iterates range(start, end - 1), omitting rows[end - 1]. Base code used range(start, end). Consequence: page_window, render_page, and summarize all silently omit the last row of every page; any single-row page renders empty (e.g. page_window(['a'], 0, 1) == [] vs base ['a']). render_page's numbering (line 43, _format_row(page_index * page_size + offset, row)) has no compensating offset, so the dropped row is lost from output entirely — a data-loss regression in every rendered page.

findings.title: Revert flipped TTL comparison in TtlCache.get
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison was changed from `< this.ttlMs` to `> this.ttlMs`, inverting the freshness check. Expired entries (elapsed > ttl) are now returned and — because the delete at line 21 only runs on the fresh branch — are never evicted, so stale values are served indefinitely and the map grows unboundedly (memory leak). Conversely, fresh entries are deleted on the next read, so every cache hit within the TTL becomes a forced miss, defeating the cache entirely.

findings.title: pruneDone: splice during forEach leaves done jobs and mutates input
findings.whyItBreaks: Two defects. (1) forEach iterates a live array: splicing index i shifts all later elements left, but the iterator advances to i+1, so the element that shifted into position i is never examined. For jobs [done, done, pending], the first splice removes job 0, forEach jumps to index 1 (the pending job), and the second done job is left in the array — the function's stated purpose fails whenever two done jobs are adjacent. (2) splice mutates the caller's array in place; the previous `filter` returned a new array, so any caller holding the original array silently loses its done jobs as a side effect.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty input after guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed guard `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` meant empty input deterministically returned 0. Now total=0 and rows.length=0, so the function returns 0/0 = NaN. Any caller rendering or accumulating the average gets NaN, which propagates silently through arithmetic and comparisons (NaN !== NaN defeats retry/rounding guards), turning an empty dataset into corrupted downstream metrics instead of a benign zero. This is a sentinel-default change on an exported public function with no in-repo caller to absorb it.

findings.title: busiest mutates caller's array via in-place sort
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous body copied the input (`[...rows].sort(...)`), leaving the caller's array untouched. The new body calls `rows.sort(...)` directly, so `busiest` reorders the caller's array in descending amount order as a side effect. Callers that rely on their own ordering (original insertion order, source query order, or any order-dependent loop or rendering after the call) now observe silently reordered data; repeated calls also re-sort arrays that are no longer in caller-controlled order. The signature `Row[] -> Row | null` promises a query, not a mutation.

findings.title: Restore numeric sort in rankScores; default sort() is lexicographic
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically. For scores [100, 99, 5]: sort() yields ["100","5","99"] i.e. [100,5,99], reverse() yields [99,5,100] — the array is not descending by value. topPlayers then takes cutoff = scores[min(n,len)-1] from this misordered array (e.g. n=1 → cutoff=99 instead of 100), so filter(p.score >= cutoff) admits player 99 while excluding the actual leader 100, and formatBoard's top-N output is wrong for any score set spanning different digit lengths (essentially every real leaderboard). The pre-change code sorted correctly with (a, b) => b - a.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in webhook signature verification
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff changed `hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature)` to `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature`. Python's str `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison runtime leaks how many leading hex characters of the attacker-supplied signature match the expected HMAC. `handle()` (app/webhook.py:13-16) uses `verify()` as the sole authorization gate for processing webhook payloads, so this is an authentication path: an attacker who can submit webhook requests can measure response timing to recover a valid signature byte-by-byte and forge authenticated payloads. The base code used `hmac.compare_digest` precisely to prevent this; the change silently removes that protection.

findings.title: Move _apply_balances call back inside the db.transaction() block
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR all three statements (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) executed atomically inside `with db.transaction():`. The diff now commits the ledger INSERT alone (line 23) and runs both balance UPDATEs outside any transaction (line 24). If either UPDATE fails or the process crashes between them, the ledger row is already committed while balances are unapplied or half-applied (e.g. debit applied, credit not), so `accounts.balance` diverges permanently from `ledger`. The exception still propagates, so a caller may retry and insert a second ledger row with no balances applied, or the ledger will report transfers whose money never moved. There is no compensation or rollback path; the pre-PR code guaranteed all-or-nothing and this diff silently removes that guarantee.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time instead of UTC, shifting day boundary by TZ offset
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation used at.getUTCFullYear()/getUTCMonth()/getUTCDate(); the new body uses at.getFullYear()/getMonth()/getDate(), which resolve in the runtime's local timezone. On any host where TZ is not UTC, an event timestamped near UTC midnight is classified into the previous or next calendar day, so billingDay/sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:7-9) return wrong values: usage is attributed to the wrong billing day and sameBillingDay says two same-UTC-day events are on different days. Because the server TZ can differ per deployment, the same Date yields different billing-day strings in different environments — a silent billing-correctness regression with no error signal.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, causing cross-tenant profile cache collisions
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level `memo` Map (src/profile.ts:7) is shared across all calls. With key = `account` only, the first call `readProfile("tenantA", "alice", ...)` caches the Profile under `"alice"`; any subsequent call `readProfile("tenantB", "alice", ...)` hits the cache at src/profile.ts:15-16 and returns tenantA's Profile (with tenantA's `tenant` and `displayName` fields) instead of fetching and caching tenantB's profile. `fetchProfile` is never invoked for tenantB, so wrong data — potentially another tenant's identity data — is served silently. The prior composite key `${tenant}:${account}` prevented this.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, `load()` threw `missing: ${key}` for absent keys, so every caller was forced to handle the failure. The added try/catch (lines 2-8) catches its own throw and returns "" instead. `load()` is an exported public function: its contract now makes failure indistinguishable from a legitimate empty-string value, and `loadAll` (src/store.ts:12) silently returns "" entries for missing keys instead of surfacing the error. Any caller persisting, comparing, or branching on the result will act on the fallback as if it were real stored data, with no error signal and no log.

findings.title: retryBackground: retries:0 means fn is never called, not one attempt
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parameter is named `retries`, which conventionally means additional attempts after the first (0 retries = exactly 1 attempt). The body uses it as the total attempt bound: with retries=0, `i < 0` is false, the loop body never runs, fn is never invoked, and retryBackground returns void with no signal — the background action is silently dropped. The shared Config interface compounds this by requiring both `maxAttempts` and `retries` on every call, so a caller cannot tell which field governs which function and must supply a field the callee ignores.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows all attempt failures, returns void on exhaustion
findings.whyItBreaks: Every thrown error is caught and discarded (lines 27-29), and when attempts are exhausted or the deadline is exceeded the function returns void — success, exhaustion, and deadline-abort are indistinguishable to every caller. As an exported API this is a present defect: each eventual caller is forced to conflate 'succeeded' with 'failed N times', and the failure is not even logged. Also `Date.now() + undefined` yields NaN if the timeout field is ever absent (e.g. external config objects), and `Date.now() > NaN` is always false, silently disabling the deadline.

findings.title: Handle numeric `value` before reading `.length` in Field
findings.whyItBreaks: The prop type is widened to `string | number`, but the body computes `value.length` directly. JavaScript numbers have no `.length` property, so `<Field value={42} />` renders `defaultValue="len=undefined"` instead of a usable label — a wrong, user-visible value on the newly-allowed input class. Under a typechecked build this is also a TS2339 error (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'`), so it either fails the build or slips through only in transpile-only mode.

findings.title: Remove step that echoes secrets.TOKEN into the workflow log
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step injects `secrets.TOKEN` as an env var and runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, sending raw secret material through a shell into the job log. GitHub's log masking is best-effort: masking is registered from the secret's stored value and fails for transformed/encoded/interpolated output, and the step also exposes the secret to anything else that reads the step's environment or captured stdout (log consumers, third-party log shippers, `set -x` expansions). The step itself has no functional effect — `make build` (line 13) does not use TOKEN, so the echo is pure debug scaffolding with a secret leak path and no benefit. If TOKEN is unset, the step silently prints `deploying with ` and the deploy proceeds anyway, hiding a missing-secret misconfiguration.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer in git() — large diffs now fail the review
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is used to capture `git diff mergeBase headSha` (github.ts:140) — the full patch for the PR. Without maxBuffer, spawnSync falls back to Node's 1 MiB default. For any PR whose diff text exceeds 1 MiB (large refactors, lockfile/generated-file changes — routine), spawnSync aborts the child with ENOBUFS: res.status becomes null and stdout/stderr are null, so `res.status !== 0` at github.ts:38 throws `git diff ... failed: ` with an empty stderr. runGithub's catch (github.ts:182-193) then posts a failure check and exits 1 — the review path is unusable for large diffs, with a misleading error message. The 64 MiB cap was deliberate: sibling functions gh (github.ts:19) and ghText (github.ts:29) still set `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64`, so the removal is inconsistent and looks accidental.

findings.title: Restore `-s read-only` sandbox flag on codex exec invocation
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line drops `"-s", "read-only"` from the args passed to `spawnSync(bin, args, ...)` at src/shared/codex.ts:23. `--sandbox` is an explicit hardening override; without it, the codex CLI falls back to its built-in default or the user's `~/.codex/config.toml`, where `sandbox_mode` may be `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access`. runCodex is used to review untrusted code (the PR under review is an injection surface), and CodexOptions exposes no way for any caller to re-impose read-only. On any machine whose codex config permits writes, the review subprocess gains filesystem write access against the repo it is supposed to only inspect — violating this tool's own stated invariant that reviewed code must never run with write access and that files created by the run are a sandbox violation. This is a silent, config-dependent removal of a security control: it passes on default-config machines and silently fails open on hardened-user-config machines.

findings.title: Diff against raw baseSha instead of merge-base admits base-branch drift
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha (line 138) comes from process.env.PR_BASE_SHA, which in the Actions context is the base branch tip (github.event.pull_request.base.sha). If main has advanced past the PR branch point, `git diff baseSha HEAD` yields (PR additions) ∪ (reverse of base-only commits): files changed on main after the branch point appear in `patch` as deletions and in `changedFiles`/`changedPaths` (lines 140-141) as PR changes. The review bundle (lines 162-172) then shows the reviewer unrelated base churn as removed code, classifyFiles mis-surfaces those files, and inline comments (line 63) anchor to files the PR never touched — wrong review output on every stale-base run. The deleted `git merge-base baseSha headSha` (old line 139) existed precisely to normalize this; the fallback path at line 138 (merge-base origin/main HEAD) is unaffected, so only the env-var path regressed.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to prevent $-pattern expansion in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace(search, replacement) interprets `$&`, `$` + backtick, `$'` and `$$` in a string replacement as special patterns; the previous `() => value` function replacers made them literal. bundle.patch and bundle JSON are attacker/PR-controlled and routinely contain such sequences (e.g. shell `echo $$`, ANSI-C `$'...'`, sed `$&`). Verified live: `"BEFORE{{P}}AFTER".replace("{{P}}", "x$&y")` yields `BEFOREx{{P}}yAFTER` (placeholder text re-injected), while the function form yields the literal `x$&y`. For {{PATCH}} (line 33), backtick-quote sequences would splice the entire prompt prefix/suffix (including reviewer policy text) into the injected patch content — a prompt-integrity/injection defect and a deterministic wrong-prompt bug, not just cosmetic. This is the CVE-2020-7663-class bug the function replacers existed to prevent.

findings.title: Fallback review submit no longer pins commit_id, can gate wrong commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary payload (src/adapters/github.ts:89) pins the review to the exact reviewed headSha via commit_id. The diff removes `commit_id=${headSha}` from the fallback form call (src/adapters/github.ts:101-112). Per GitHub's API, omitting commit_id on POST /pulls/{n}/reviews defaults to the current branch head. The fallback path runs exactly when the primary (pinned, comment-bearing) submission fails; if the PR head advanced while the review was being generated, the fallback now submits the verdict — including REQUEST_CHANGES, which is a merge-gating signal — against a commit the reviewer never saw, mis-attributing and mis-gating the newer commit. headSha is resolved once at src/adapters/github.ts:141, well before this call, so the race is real on long review runs.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently launders malformed findings into default-valued valid ones
findings.whyItBreaks: Base threw `malformed finding: ...` for any invalid severity/category/empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix or non-positive lineStart/lineEnd, and normalizeReview's `strict` parameter let callers either propagate those throws or explicitly drop bad findings. Head unconditionally coerces: unknown severity becomes 'P1', invalid category becomes 'bug', empty file becomes '', lineStart/lineEnd become 0, missing title becomes 'Untitled finding', and empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix pass through. Since normalizeFinding/normalizeReview are exported public API that sanitize untrusted review-agent output (no other callers exist in-repo; grep confirms only the internal map at line 131), every downstream consumer is forced to conflate a malformed/hostile finding with a real one: it cannot detect failure, it receives fabricated P1-severity findings with empty file and zero line numbers that can no longer be anchored to code, and the pipeline cannot distinguish 'agent produced no valid findings' from 'agent output was corrupt'. For a review gate that feeds verdicts, silently manufacturing findings from garbage output is a correctness and integrity defect, not cleanup.

findings.title: Restore repo context for `gh pr view` before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step (lines 26-40) runs before 'Checkout PR head' (line 42-46), so the workspace contains no git repository. `gh` resolves its repository only from `-R/--repo`, the `GH_REPO` env var, or a git remote in the current directory; it does not infer the repo from `GH_TOKEN`. After this change, on the workflow_dispatch path (EVENT_HEAD empty, the only path that reaches line 38-39) `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` fails with 'no current repository'. Because the call sits inside `$(...)` fed to `echo`, the echo still succeeds: the step goes green while writing `head=` and `base=` empty into GITHUB_OUTPUT. The following checkout then falls back to the default branch (ref: '') and the Needlefish review step receives empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA — the manual review path is broken and fails silently rather than erroring loudly.

findings.title: normalizeReview coerces malformed output into empty pass-shaped review
findings.whyItBreaks: Base f4d6114 threw explicit errors for non-object input, missing/non-string summary, or missing/non-array findings/checked/residual_risks (base schema.ts:113-127). The new body replaces every throw with a default: any falsy, non-object, or field-missing value (undefined, "", 42, {findings: {}}) returns a well-formed RawReview with findings=[], checked=[], residual_risks=[]. Empty findings + empty residual_risks is exactly the 'pass with no blocking risks' sentinel, so a failed or truncated agent run becomes indistinguishable from a legitimate clean approval — the caller is forced to conflate failure with a real pass and can approve the PR on garbage input. As an exported contract, every eventual caller must treat the fallback as real regardless of in-repo callers today.

findings.title: Manual dispatch reviews wrong code: empty PR shas and base-branch checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch (the only mode the deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step's else-branch existed for), `github.event.pull_request.*` is empty. Line 29's `github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` then checks out the dispatch-time ref (typically the base branch), and lines 45-46 export `PR_BASE_SHA=''` and `PR_HEAD_SHA=''`. The base revision of this job resolved head/base/base_ref via `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` exactly for this case. Now `tsx src/cli.ts --github --pr <N>` runs from the wrong tree (in self-review mode, the base branch's src/, i.e. the tool reviewing itself pre-change, missing any changes to the reviewer itself) with empty sentinel shas. Additionally, line 35's `BASE_REF` falls back to the hardcoded 'main' rather than the PR's actual base.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer in git() to avoid ENOBUFS on diffs over 1MB
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1048576 bytes (1 MiB). runLocal calls git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at line 100 and git(["diff", "--name-only", ...]) at line 101; large-but-legitimate diffs (lockfiles, vendored or generated code) routinely exceed 1MB of patch text. When output exceeds maxBuffer, spawnSync kills the process: res.status becomes null and the real failure signal lands in res.error, which this code never reads. The check `if (res.status !== 0)` at line 12 then throws `git diff <sha> <sha> failed:` with empty stderr — the review aborts with a message that hides ENOBUFS entirely, making local review unusable on exactly the large diffs a review agent must handle. The unchanged gh() wrapper at lines 33-37 still sets maxBuffer: 64MB, confirming the removed value in git() was intentional.

findings.title: Pass --repo <repo> to gh pr diff; it currently relies on ambient repo context
findings.whyItBreaks: Every other gh call addresses the repo explicitly (e.g. `api repos/${repo}/pulls/${prNumber}` at line 136-139, `repos/${repo}/check-runs` at line 121), so the adapter works regardless of the process working directory. `gh pr diff <n>` instead resolves the repo from the *process* cwd's git remotes (or GH_REPO); runGithub accepts a separate `cwd` for git commands, so whenever the process cwd is not the reviewed repo (or the remote is absent/unauthenticated for that host), this call throws `gh pr diff failed: none of the git remotes...` and the entire review aborts on the new error path — a regression versus the previous `git diff baseSha HEAD`, which used the explicit cwd.

findings.title: changedFiles uses 2-dot diff while patch is 3-dot; bases diverge when base branch moves
findings.whyItBreaks: `gh pr diff` (line 143) computes merge-base(base, head)...head, but `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` (line 144 → line 57: `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD`) uses baseSha (= pr.base.sha, the base-branch tip) two-dot. When the base branch has advanced past the fork point, the two sets differ: changedFiles/classifyFiles (line 144-145, feeds bundle.changedFiles) contains upstream-only files absent from the patch, and inlineComments (line 63) anchors comments against that wrong set. The bundle also hands the reviewer baseSha/headSha while patch is 3-dot, so any `git diff base head` cross-check by the review agent mismatches the provided diff. Previously patch and changedFiles shared one basis and were consistent.

findings.title: Review-pipeline error now reports neutral check, unblocking required-check gates
findings.whyItBreaks: The error path previously posted conclusion "failure"; it now posts "neutral" (line 191). If the branch protection required-check "Needlefish" is enforced, neutral is a non-blocking conclusion, so a crashed/errored review silently stops blocking merges — while the check's own summary says "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR" and line 196 still sets exitCode 1, contradicting the posted state. The gate's intent (do not pass an unreviewed PR) is defeated on the API-reported status.

findings.title: Review workflow now executes untrusted PR-head code, defeating self-review protection
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version checked out the reviewer tool from ref `main` (path `needlefish`) and ran it only against the untrusted PR head checkout (`target`). The new version checks out the PR head once and runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts --github ...` directly from that checkout (line 59), i.e. the CI job executes arbitrary code shipped by the PR itself. Any pull request (including from a fork contributor once the `head.repo.full_name == github.repository` check on line 24 is satisfied, or any routine same-repo PR) can modify `src/cli.ts` to force its own review to PASS, suppress findings, or exfiltrate `GH_TOKEN` (which has `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write`, lines 18-19) and other runner-accessible secrets. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 51) additionally runs postinstall scripts from the untrusted checkout. The deleted comment explicitly stated this pattern existed to 'prevent a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool'; this repo IS the tool, so this is precisely the case where the protection matters most. The same-repo-only guard (line 24) does not mitigate: same-repo PRs are the primary attack channel.

findings.title: Comment points users to README.md template that does not exist in the repo
findings.whyItBreaks: The new comment (lines 3-5) directs users of OTHER repos to 'the generic template in README.md'. `git ls-tree -r` at both base and head shows the repo tree contains only `.github/workflows/review.yml` and `.needlefish/answers.json` — no README.md exists, so downstream users copying this workflow for another repo are pointed at documentation that does not exist, and the trusted-tool pattern they need (per the finding above) has no documented source.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Silently downgrade non-canonical severities to P3 instead of normalizing
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code normalized raw severity via String(...).trim().toUpperCase(), so LLM-produced values like "p1" or " P0 " were accepted and preserved. The changed code checks SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity) on the raw value directly, so "p1" fails the check and is silently replaced with the new default "P3" (base default was "P1"). Concrete wrong behavior: normalizeFinding({severity: "p0", ...}) returned severity "P0" before this PR and returns "P3" after — a real blocker-severity finding is rewritten to the lowest severity with no error. normalizeReview (line 132) maps every raw finding through this function, and the review pipeline's validator gates on severity per its own policy (P0/P1/P2 findings require confidence >= 0.70; P3 bypasses that gate), so a lowercase-cased severe finding both survives validation it should have failed and is reported at the wrong priority. The P1→P3 default change compounds this: any malformed severity now defaults to the least-blocking class instead of an escalation class.

findings.title: Restore GH_TOKEN scrub before spawning codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version copied process.env and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawnSync, deliberately withholding GitHub credentials from the codex subprocess. The head version omits `env` entirely (lines 23-29), so spawnSync inherits the full parent environment by default — any GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN present (e.g. in CI, where runCodex-style review agents typically run) is now readable by the codex CLI and anything it executes. The prompt passed via `input` can carry untrusted repo content (the review pipeline's stated injection surface), so this converts a hardening control into live credential exposure: the subprocess can read the tokens from its own environment regardless of the `-s read-only` sandbox, which governs file access, not env vars. `rg` confirms no other code in the repo scrubs or consumes these variables, so this deleted block was the only defense.

findings.title: Restore fork guard: workflow now runs untrusted fork code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the workflow's only fork-protection gate. With it removed, any `pull_request` event from an external fork now starts the `review` job on the `self-hosted` runner, which then (1) checks out the fork's head (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, line 23), (2) runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) executing arbitrary postinstall scripts from the untrusted fork, and (3) executes `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) — all under `shell: zsh -l`, a login shell on a persistent self-hosted machine that typically carries ambient host access and cross-run cached state. This is the canonical GitHub Actions fork-execution supply-chain exposure. Additionally, even the review itself is broken on fork PRs: `GITHUB_TOKEN` is force-downgraded to read-only for fork runs regardless of the declared `pull-requests: write` (line 13), so the tool's review post would 403 — the job burns runner capacity on untrusted code and still cannot deliver its output.

findings.title: Silently override valid env value 0 for runner timeout grace/give-up
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code accepted 0 (parsed >= 0). After the change, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 (legit config: escalate to SIGKILL immediately, no grace) is silently replaced by the 5000ms default @line 5, and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 (stop waiting for close immediately after SIGKILL) by 2000ms @line 9. Deployments that set 0 now wait 5s/2s before hard-killing or giving up, a user-visible behavior change on upgrade with no signal that the configured value was ignored.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual risks (incl. blocks=true) are silently dropped
findings.whyItBreaks: Base collected each deep pass's residual risks (`residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)`) and fed them to the critic via candidateMerged.residual_risks, so a sub-reviewer's 'blocks:true' gap reached deriveVerdict and blocked the verdict. Head hardcodes `residual_risks: []` (review.ts:113) and drops the collection. The critic can only preserve candidate residual risks, never invent them, so every blocking evidence gap reported by a deep reviewer (e.g. 'cannot trace sentinel on a live path') vanishes and deriveVerdict (review.ts:122) can emit a PASS verdict on a review that base policy required to block. Failure and 'no gaps' are now indistinguishable to the verdict consumer.

findings.title: Changed files not covered by selected hotspots are silently skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: Base added a 'tail-coverage' hotspot so every changed file — including ones the map pass omitted and ones dropped by `slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (review.ts:93) — was deep-reviewed; the deleted comment stated 'never silently skip a changed file'. Head removes it: any changed file not in a selected hotspot receives zero deep review, and nothing (checked entry or residual risk) records the skip. For a merge-gating review agent, a changed file escaping review with no trace is a silent coverage regression.

findings.title: One malformed deep-pass output now aborts the entire review
findings.whyItBreaks: Base wrapped each deep pass in try/catch: a failed pass (LLM malformed JSON, codex error) recorded `[name] DEEP PASS FAILED` in checked and a `blocks:true` residual, and the remaining hotspots still ran. Head calls runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview unguarded: any single transient failure throws out of review(), discarding findings from all already-completed hotspots and making the whole PR review unusable on non-deterministic LLM output. This is only tolerable because finding #1's residual plumbing was removed; combined, a sub-reviewer failure either kills everything (this) or disappears entirely (that).

findings.title: Coarser dedup key can merge two distinct findings into one
findings.whyItBreaks: The dedup key dropped the `norm(f.whyItBreaks).slice(0, 80)` component. Two genuinely distinct findings at the same file+lineStart+category with titles sharing the same normalized 60-char prefix (e.g. 'missing validation on empty input' for two different failure modes reported by different deep passes) now collapse to the higher-severity one and the other is silently dropped — in a review agent, losing a real finding is the product defect.

findings.title: Restore focus injection in reviewLarge; {{FOCUS}} placeholder now leaks unsubstituted
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` without modifying prompts/deep.md in the same diff, so if the (unchanged) template still contains the {{FOCUS}} token, every large-PR deep-review prompt is sent containing the literal string {{FOCUS}} and the user's focus text is silently ignored. Independently of the placeholder: reviewSmall (review.ts:52-55) still serializes the whole bundle, so focus/deep are honored for small PRs but silently dropped for large PRs (the mapBundle at 83-89 also no longer carries focus/deep) — the exact path handling the largest, highest-risk diffs. Users get no signal their review directive was discarded.

findings.title: formatDuration emits "60s" / "Nm 60s" when sub-second rounding carries
findings.whyItBreaks: seconds is rounded after the minute split, so ms values whose sub-minute remainder rounds up to 60 (e.g. 59_500–59_999 or 119_600–119_999) produce malformed report output: the old code returned "1m 0s" / "2m 0s", the new code returns "60s" / "1m 60s". Verified by substitution: newFmt(59600)="60s", newFmt(119600)="1m 60s", newFmt(599500)="9m 60s", while oldFmt returned valid "1m 0s"/"2m 0s"/"10m 0s" for the same inputs. These strings are rendered into the review report's per-call stats and total line (render.ts:75,80), i.e. user-visible output.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 and empty input, breaking its validation contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes the guard accept 0. Since `Number('')` and `Number('   ')` coerce to 0, empty/blank CLI or config inputs are now silently accepted as the value 0 as well. The exported function's name (`parsePositiveInteger`) and its error text (`requires a positive integer`) still promise strict positive-integer validation; callers of this shared module (e.g. values feeding `RunnerOptions.timeoutMs`) will receive 0 where the contract promises rejection, and any consumer that divides by, loops on, or uses the value as a timeout/retry count gets wrong behavior instead of the validation error it relies on. This is TRIGGER C: the contract carrier (exported name + error message @src/shared/runner.ts:30-33) promises positive-integer validation; the body (line 32) now returns 0. The promised validation behavior affects the data returned to callers, so it is a defect regardless of current in-repo caller count.
